title: Cell Grid With Two-Term Formulas
statement:
Build a tiny spreadsheet. It has 26 columns named A to Z and rows rows numbered from 1. A cell is named by its column letter followed by its row number, like "C7" or "B120". Every cell starts at 0.

  • Sheet(rows) creates the grid with every cell set to 0.
  • setCell(cell, value) stores value in that cell.
  • resetCell(cell) sets that cell back to 0.
  • getValue(formula) evaluates a formula of the exact form "=X+Y" and returns the result. Each of X and Y is either a non-negative whole number or a cell name; a cell name stands for the cell's current value.

Formulas are evaluated on the spot; they are not stored in cells. Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the sheet, and the expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: Plain numbers add directly. After B2 is reset it counts as 0 again, so only C3's 2 remains.
A1 and A10 are different cells: read the whole row number, not just its first digit.

constraints: 0 ≤ value ≤ 100 000, and every number inside a formula is in the same range
Every cell name is valid for the sheet; every formula has the form "=X+Y"
hints: You need to store a number per cell and read it back by name. What is the simplest structure keyed by a name?
A formula always has two terms. Split after the = on the +, and decide for each term whether it starts with a letter or a digit.
For a fixed-size grid you can also turn "C7" into indexes: column 'C' − 'A', row 7 − 1. A hash map keyed by the name avoids that and stores only cells that were set.

explain.intuition:
This is a storage problem with a small parser on top. Each cell is a number that can be set, reset and read. A hash map from cell name to value does all three in O(1), and a missing key simply means 0, so the sheet never has to allocate the full grid. That is the same reason a web spreadsheet keeps a sparse map of filled cells instead of a giant 2D array.

The formula is always two terms joined by +. Strip the =, split on +, and resolve each term: if its first character is a letter it is a cell name, otherwise it is a number.
steps: Keep a map cells from cell name to value.
setCell: store the value under the name.
getValue: take the formula after =, split on +, resolve each term (letter first → map lookup with default 0, otherwise parse the number) and return the sum.
pitfalls: Reading only one digit of the row number, so A10 and A1 collide.
Throwing or returning NaN for a cell that was never set. Unset cells are 0.
Treating every term as a cell name (or every term as a number). Each term must be checked on its own.

complexity.time: O(1) per operation (formula length is constant)

solutions.title: Full 2D array
solutions.idea: Allocate a rows × 26 grid. Turn a cell name into a row and a column index.
solutions.time: O(1) per operation, O(rows) to create

solutions.title: Sparse hash map
solutions.idea: Store only the cells that hold a value. A missing name reads as 0.

followups: Cells can now hold formulas that refer to other cells, and reads must reflect later changes. How do you store and evaluate them, and how do you detect a cycle?
Formulas may contain any number of terms, such as "=A1+B2+7+C3". What changes?
